column2: the alarm goes off on a school morning
column3: get up at the first alarm instead of pressing snooze again and again
column4: snoozing makes you rush, skip breakfast and arrive late and stressed

column2: packing the school bag
column3: pack it the night before: homework, books, pencil case, water bottle, lunch and anything for special days such as PE kit
column4: in the morning there is little time and forgotten things are hard to fetch from school

column2: it is PE day
column3: wear or pack the sports clothes and trainers the school asks for and tie long hair back
column4: the right clothes keep you safe and comfortable when you run and jump

column2: not wanting to go to school one morning
column3: tell a parent honestly why, for example a worry, a quarrel or feeling ill, rather than pretending
column4: a real problem can only be fixed if an adult knows about it

column2: skipping breakfast because you are in a hurry
column3: eat at least something simple such as toast, fruit or cereal before school
column4: the brain needs food to concentrate and you may feel tired or grumpy by mid-morning

column2: a note or form from school has to be signed
column3: give it to a parent on the same day and bring it back by the date written on it
column4: trips and activities often cannot go ahead for you without the signed form

column2: the bell rings at the start of the day
column3: go to your line or classroom straight away and get ready to listen
column4: lessons start on time and the teacher may give important news at the beginning

column2: taking the register or roll call
column3: answer clearly when your name is called, for example «here» or «present»
column4: the school must know exactly which children are in the building in case of an emergency

column2: arriving late to school
column3: go to the school office first to sign in, then go to class quietly and say sorry for being late
column4: the office must record that you are on site, and coming in quietly disturbs the class less

column2: the school timetable or schedule
column3: learn which subject comes when and on which days, and check it the night before
column4: you will bring the right things and know where to be

column2: moving between classrooms in the corridor
column3: walk on the correct side, do not run, and keep your voice low
column4: corridors are crowded and running causes collisions and falls

column2: the fire alarm goes off
column3: stop what you are doing, leave your things, line up quietly and follow the teacher to the meeting point outside
column4: a calm, quick evacuation lets everyone get out safely and be counted

column2: a lockdown drill
column3: stay silent, follow the teacher's instructions exactly and stay away from doors and windows until told it is over
column4: drills practise keeping everyone safe if there is ever a danger outside the classroom

column2: an earthquake drill in New Zealand or the western USA
column3: drop, cover under a desk and hold on until the shaking stops
column4: falling objects cause most injuries and a sturdy desk protects your head

column2: the school assembly
column3: sit quietly, listen to the speakers and clap politely at the end
column4: assembly brings the whole school together and good manners show respect to the speakers

column2: the end of the school day
column3: wait at the agreed place for the adult who collects you and never leave with someone who is not on your list
column4: the school and your family must always know who you are with

column2: your usual adult does not come to pick you up
column3: go back into the school office and tell a teacher; do not walk off or accept a lift from someone you were not told about
column4: the school can phone your family and keep you safe until someone arrives

column2: the school bus
column3: be at the stop a few minutes early, wait well back from the road, stay seated and do not distract the driver
column4: the bus will not wait long, and a distracted driver or a child in the aisle can cause an accident

column2: crossing the road outside school
column3: use the crossing with the crossing guard or lollipop lady and wait for their signal
column4: cars near schools are many and drivers may not see small children

column2: walking to school alone for the first time
column3: agree the route with a parent, keep to it, and go straight to school without stopping
column4: parents know where to look for you if anything goes wrong

column2: feeling ill during a lesson
column3: tell the teacher and ask to go to the school nurse or office
column4: the school can look after you and phone your family if you need to go home

column2: needing the toilet during a lesson
column3: ask the teacher politely, then go and come back quickly
column4: the teacher needs to know where every child is

column2: losing a jumper or water bottle at school
column3: look in the lost property box and write your name on your things
column4: lost things with names on them are returned quickly

column2: bringing a mobile phone to school
column3: follow the school rule, usually keeping it switched off in your bag or handing it in
column4: phones distract from lessons and many schools allow them only for emergencies

column2: bringing something valuable or a toy to school
column3: leave expensive toys and money at home unless the teacher asked for them
column4: things can get lost, broken or cause arguments at school

column2: wearing the school uniform
column3: wear it neatly and correctly, as your school asks
column4: uniforms are common in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand and show you belong to the school; many US schools have a dress code instead

column2: a non-uniform or dress-up day
column3: check the theme and bring the small donation if one is asked for
column4: such days usually raise money for charity and are fun to join

column2: the teacher is talking to the class
column3: stop talking, look at the teacher and listen
column4: you will miss instructions and disturb others if you chat

column2: wanting to say something in class
column3: put your hand up and wait to be asked
column4: if everyone shouts at once nobody can be heard

column2: a classmate is answering a question
column3: listen without interrupting or laughing, even if the answer is wrong
column4: everyone needs to feel safe to try, including you

column2: finishing your work early
column3: check it, then do the extra task the teacher set or read quietly
column4: this uses the time well and does not disturb others still working

column2: borrowing a classmate's pencil or rubber
column3: ask first and give it back when you finish
column4: it belongs to them and they may need it

column2: keeping your desk or table tidy
column3: put books, pencils and papers back where they belong at the end of the lesson
column4: you will find things quickly and the room stays safe and pleasant

column2: using scissors in class
column3: carry them closed with the points down, and cut away from your fingers
column4: scissors can cut you or others if handled carelessly

column2: the class pet
column3: feed and handle it only as the teacher shows you and wash your hands afterwards
column4: animals can be hurt by rough handling and can carry germs

column2: a classmate is making noise and you cannot concentrate
column3: ask them kindly to be quiet, and tell the teacher if it continues
column4: a calm request often works, and the teacher can help if it does not

column2: the teacher tells the class off for something you did not do
column3: stay calm and politely explain later, in private if possible
column4: arguing in front of the class makes things worse; a calm talk is more likely to be heard

column2: being given a class job such as handing out books
column3: do it carefully and on time
column4: class jobs teach responsibility and help the whole class

column2: a classmate is new to the school
column3: say hello, show them where things are and invite them to play
column4: starting a new school is hard and a friendly face helps a lot

column2: a classmate speaks little English yet
column3: speak slowly, use gestures and pictures, and be patient
column4: they are learning a new language and will understand more every week

column2: whispering a secret about someone in class
column3: do not gossip about others
column4: it hurts feelings and spreads untrue stories

column2: the classroom computer or tablet
column3: use it only for what the teacher allowed and never change settings or open other sites
column4: school devices are shared and filters are there to keep you safe online

column2: throwing things in the classroom
column3: never throw objects indoors, even as a joke
column4: things can hit eyes and faces and break windows

column2: swinging back on your chair
column3: keep all four chair legs on the floor
column4: chairs tip over easily and cause head injuries

column2: getting homework from the teacher
column3: write down what to do and when it is due in your planner or homework diary
column4: it is easy to forget by the evening

column2: when to do homework
column3: do it at the same time each day, after a short break and a snack, and before screens
column4: a routine makes starting easier and you are less tired than late in the evening

column2: where to do homework
column3: sit at a clear table with good light, away from the TV and with the phone in another room
column4: distractions make homework take twice as long

column2: not understanding the homework
column3: reread the task, look at your class notes, then ask a parent to explain the question, not to do it for you
column4: the homework is to help you learn, and the teacher needs to see what you can do

column2: a parent offers to do the homework for you
column3: thank them but do it yourself and ask only for hints
column4: if they do it, you learn nothing and the teacher cannot see what you need help with

column2: forgetting to do homework
column3: tell the teacher honestly before the lesson and offer to hand it in the next day
column4: honesty keeps trust; making excuses or lying makes it worse when it is found out

column2: a big project due in three weeks
column3: split it into small steps and write a date for each step on the calendar
column4: leaving it to the last night leads to rushed, poor work and stress

column2: copying a friend's homework
column3: do your own work and ask the friend to explain how they did it instead
column4: copying is cheating and you will not know how to do it in the test

column2: homework copied from the internet
column3: write in your own words and say where you found the facts
column4: copying text and passing it off as yours is plagiarism, a kind of cheating

column2: using an AI chatbot for homework
column3: use it only if the teacher allows, and only to understand, never to write the answer for you
column4: the teacher wants to see your thinking, and chatbots can be confidently wrong

column2: spelling words for the week
column3: practise a few each day by look, say, cover, write, check
column4: short daily practice sticks in memory far better than one long session

column2: times tables practice
column3: say and write them a little every day and test yourself out of order
column4: knowing times tables by heart makes harder maths much faster

column2: reading every evening
column3: read for about twenty minutes and write it in the reading record
column4: daily reading makes you a faster, better reader and builds vocabulary

column2: being too tired to finish homework
column3: stop, tell a parent, and let the teacher know with a note
column4: working when exhausted gives poor results, and teachers would rather know

column2: homework that takes far too long every night
column3: tell a parent so they can talk to the teacher
column4: homework is meant to be a set amount of time, and the teacher may adjust it

column2: losing a worksheet
column3: ask a classmate or the teacher for another copy, or check the school website
column4: most teachers keep spare copies and online versions

column2: messy handwriting in homework
column3: write slowly enough that others can read it
column4: if the teacher cannot read the answer it cannot be marked right

column2: a spelling or maths test is announced
column3: revise a little on several days before the test, not only the night before
column4: spreading revision out helps you remember for longer

column2: the night before a test
column3: pack what you need and go to bed on time instead of staying up late
column4: a rested brain thinks and remembers much better

column2: feeling nervous before a test
column3: take a few slow deep breaths and remind yourself that you prepared
column4: a little nervousness is normal and slow breathing calms the body

column2: starting a test
column3: write your name, read every question carefully and do the ones you know first
column4: you get marks for what you can do and save time for the hard ones

column2: getting stuck on one test question
column3: move on and come back to it at the end
column4: spending all the time on one question leaves no time for the others

column2: finishing a test early
column3: check your answers and make sure you answered every question
column4: checking catches careless mistakes

column2: looking at a neighbour's paper in a test
column3: keep your eyes on your own paper
column4: copying is cheating; the test must show what you know

column2: a friend asks you to show your answers in a test
column3: say no quietly and cover your paper
column4: helping someone cheat gets you both in trouble and does not help them learn

column2: a teacher leaves the room during a test
column3: keep working silently on your own paper
column4: honesty matters most when nobody is watching

column2: national tests such as SATs in England or NAPLAN in Australia
column3: do your best, but know they check how the school teaches as well as what you know
column4: worrying too much helps nobody, and one test does not decide your future

column2: getting a lower mark than you hoped
column3: look at what you got wrong and ask how to improve
column4: the mark shows what to practise next, not how clever you are forever

column2: getting a high mark
column3: be glad but do not boast to classmates who did worse
column4: bragging makes others feel bad

column2: being asked by others what mark you got
column3: you may tell or politely keep it private
column4: marks are personal and nobody has to share them

column2: the report card or school report
column3: read it with a parent and talk about one thing to keep and one thing to improve
column4: reports show strengths and next steps

column2: wanting to change a bad mark on a test before parents see it
column3: never change marks or forge a parent's signature; show it honestly
column4: forging is dishonest and the trouble is much bigger when it is found out

column2: making a mistake in class work
column3: cross it out neatly or fix it, and try again
column4: mistakes are how everyone learns; nobody learns without them

column2: feeling stupid after a wrong answer
column3: remember that the wrong answer shows you what to learn next
column4: the brain grows by struggling with things it does not yet know

column2: a classmate laughs at your mistake
column3: calmly say it is not kind, and tell the teacher if it continues
column4: laughing at mistakes stops people trying

column2: you laughed at someone's mistake
column3: say sorry to them
column4: you hurt their feelings and an apology helps put it right

column2: the teacher makes a mistake on the board
column3: politely put up your hand and say you think there may be an error
column4: teachers are human and most are glad to be helped

column2: accidentally breaking something in the classroom
column3: tell the teacher straight away
column4: it can be cleaned up safely, and owning up is more respected than hiding it

column2: being blamed for a classmate's mistake
column3: explain calmly what really happened
column4: the truth told calmly is usually believed

column2: giving up after the first try
column3: try again in a different way or ask for a hint
column4: most skills need many tries before they work

column2: not understanding what the teacher explained
column3: put up your hand and ask, or ask at the end of the lesson
column4: if you do not understand, many others probably do not either

column2: being afraid that a question is silly
column3: ask anyway; teachers like questions
column4: asking is the fastest way to learn

column2: how to ask a good question
column3: say what you already understand and exactly which part confuses you
column4: a precise question gets a precise answer

column2: not knowing a word
column3: ask its meaning or look it up in a dictionary
column4: each new word you learn helps you read everything else

column2: a question that is not about the lesson
column3: save it for break time or the end of the lesson
column4: the class needs to stay on the lesson topic

column2: wanting to know more about a topic
column3: ask the teacher for a good book or website and visit the library
column4: curiosity is how people become experts

column2: being put in a group with children you do not usually play with
column3: be friendly and work together well
column4: you can learn from everyone and may make new friends

column2: one child in the group does all the talking
column3: suggest that everyone takes a turn to share an idea
column4: the best results come when every idea is heard

column2: one child in the group does no work
column3: kindly invite them to do a specific part, and tell the teacher if it continues
column4: giving someone a clear job often helps them join in

column2: disagreeing about how to do a group task
column3: listen to each idea, then vote or try a mix of ideas
column4: fair ways of deciding stop quarrels

column2: your idea is not chosen by the group
column3: accept it and help with the chosen idea
column4: being a good team member matters more than winning every time

column2: dividing jobs in a group project
column3: give each person a clear role, such as writer, drawer, timekeeper or presenter
column4: everyone knows what to do and the work is fair

column2: a partner gets the answer wrong
column3: help them see the mistake kindly without making them feel bad
column4: kind help makes the partner willing to keep trying

column2: presenting to the class
column3: practise beforehand, speak slowly and loudly, and look at the audience
column4: practice makes you less nervous and the audience understands you

column2: working with a partner in pairs
column3: take turns, listen and share the work
column4: both of you learn and the job is fair

column2: someone in the group is left out
column3: invite them in and ask for their idea
column4: being left out hurts, and including everyone is kind

column2: greeting the teacher in the morning
column3: say good morning and use their name, such as Mrs Smith or Mr Jones
column4: good manners make a good start to the day

column2: how to address teachers
column3: use Mr, Mrs, Ms or Miss with the surname, or Sir and Miss in many British schools
column4: calling teachers by their first name is usually seen as rude at school

column2: a substitute or relief teacher takes the class
column3: behave just as well as with your own teacher and help them with names and routines
column4: they are your teacher for the day and deserve the same respect

column2: the head teacher or principal comes into the class
column3: stop and listen politely
column4: the head teacher leads the school

column2: the teaching assistant or aide
column3: listen to them and treat them like a teacher
column4: they help teach and look after the class

column2: the school caretaker, janitor, cleaners and lunch staff
column3: say thank you and help keep the school tidy
column4: they work hard to keep the school clean and running

column2: the school receptionist or office staff
column3: go to them if you are late, hurt, ill or need to phone home
column4: they look after messages and contact families

column2: the school nurse or first aider
column3: go to them when you are hurt or feel ill
column4: they know first aid and when to call your family

column2: being worried or sad about something at home or school
column3: tell a trusted adult, such as your teacher, the school counsellor or a parent
column4: adults at school are there to help, and worries are lighter when shared

column2: an adult at school asks you to keep a secret that makes you uncomfortable
column3: do not keep it; tell a parent or another trusted adult
column4: safe adults never ask children to keep secrets that worry them

column2: a stranger in the school grounds without a visitor badge
column3: tell a teacher straight away and do not go with them
column4: visitors must sign in at the office and wear a badge

column2: a teacher seems unfair to you
column3: talk calmly to the teacher, or ask a parent to talk to them
column4: problems are solved by talking, not by being rude

column2: thanking a teacher at the end of the year
column3: a card or a few kind words are enough
column4: teachers value thanks; expensive gifts are not needed

column2: parent–teacher evenings or conferences
column3: know that your parents and teacher talk about how you are doing
column4: they work together to help you learn

column2: being told off by a teacher
column3: listen, say sorry if you were wrong, and do not answer back rudely
column4: answering back makes the trouble bigger

column2: getting a detention or losing play time
column3: accept it and think about what to do differently
column4: consequences help people change behaviour

column2: the bell rings at the end of break
column3: stop playing straight away and line up
column4: lessons must start on time

column2: wanting to join a game others are playing
column3: ask «can I play?» and accept the rules of the game
column4: asking politely is the best way to join in

column2: someone asks to join your game
column3: say yes whenever possible
column4: being left out hurts and more players can be more fun

column2: being left out of a game
column3: ask someone else to play, or go to a teacher on duty
column4: there are always other children looking for a friend

column2: a child with nobody to play with
column3: invite them to play with you
column4: a lonely child will remember your kindness

column2: a game of tag gets too rough
column3: stop and say the game needs to be gentler; tell the duty teacher if it continues
column4: rough games lead to injuries and fights

column2: someone falls and gets hurt
column3: tell the teacher on duty and stay with the child
column4: they may need first aid

column2: seeing someone being bullied
column3: do not join in; tell a teacher, and be kind to the child who was bullied
column4: bullying is repeated hurting on purpose and adults can stop it

column2: being bullied yourself
column3: tell a trusted adult and keep telling until it stops
column4: bullying is never your fault and you should not deal with it alone

column2: arguing over the rules of a game
column3: agree on the rules before starting, or use rock, paper, scissors to decide
column4: clear rules stop quarrels

column2: losing a game
column3: say «well played» to the winner and do not sulk
column4: being a good loser makes others want to play with you

column2: winning a game
column3: say «good game» and do not tease the losers
column4: being a good winner keeps friendships

column2: climbing equipment
column3: use one hand per rung, take turns and do not push
column4: falls from height cause broken bones

column2: playing in the sun in Australia or New Zealand
column3: wear a school hat and sunscreen: «no hat, no play»
column4: the sun there is very strong and sunburn raises skin-cancer risk

column2: the playground is icy or snowy
column3: walk carefully and do not throw snowballs at faces or with ice in them
column4: ice is slippery and icy snowballs can injure eyes

column2: someone takes your ball or toy
column3: ask for it back politely, then tell a teacher
column4: grabbing back starts fights

column2: playing a game with a ball near windows
column3: play ball games only in the allowed area
column4: balls break windows and hit people

column2: a wasp or bee comes near at break
column3: stay calm, move away slowly and do not swat it
column4: swatting makes stings more likely

column2: waiting in the lunch queue
column3: wait your turn and do not push in
column4: pushing in is unfair to everyone waiting

column2: eating lunch at school
column3: sit down to eat, chew with your mouth closed and do not shout
column4: good table manners make lunch pleasant for everyone

column2: a classmate has a food allergy
column3: never share food with them, and wash hands after eating nuts
column4: some allergies, such as to peanuts, can be deadly

column2: many schools are nut-free
column3: do not bring nuts or peanut butter if the school asks you not to
column4: tiny traces can harm a child with a severe allergy

column2: not liking the school lunch
column3: try a little and politely leave the rest, or talk to parents about packed lunch
column4: trying new food is good, and parents can help find a solution

column2: forgetting your lunch
column3: tell the teacher or office so they can help
column4: schools can phone home or provide something to eat

column2: spilling a drink in the lunch hall
column3: tell a lunch supervisor and help clean it up
column4: wet floors make people slip

column2: washing hands before lunch
column3: wash with soap for about twenty seconds
column4: hands carry germs that cause stomach upsets and colds

column2: leftover rubbish after lunch
column3: put it in the right bin: recycling, compost or general waste
column4: keeping the school clean and recycling helps the environment

column2: someone has no lunch or very little
column3: tell a teacher quietly rather than sharing in a way that embarrasses them
column4: the school can help privately; many schools offer free school meals

column2: trading food with friends
column3: do it only if your school allows it and nobody has allergies
column4: swapping food can be risky for children with allergies

column2: going on a school trip
column3: bring the signed permission slip, a packed lunch, water and clothes for the weather
column4: you cannot go without permission and the day may be long and outdoors

column2: being given a trip buddy
column3: stay with your buddy all day and tell the teacher if you get separated
column4: a buddy system means nobody is lost without someone noticing

column2: getting lost on a trip
column3: stay where you are, or go to a staff member in uniform, a police officer or a mother with children, and say you are with a school group
column4: staying still makes you easier to find, and these adults can contact your teacher

column2: the coach or bus on a trip
column3: wear the seatbelt, stay seated and keep the bus tidy
column4: seatbelts save lives in a crash

column2: feeling travel sick on the bus
column3: tell the teacher early, sit near the front and look out of the window at the horizon
column4: the teacher can help before you are sick

column2: a museum or gallery visit
column3: walk, talk quietly and do not touch exhibits unless a sign allows it
column4: exhibits are precious and can be damaged by hands

column2: a trip to a farm
column3: do not touch animals without permission and wash hands well afterwards
column4: farm animals can carry germs such as E. coli

column2: buying souvenirs on a trip
column3: decide before you go how much of your money to spend and keep it safe
column4: it is easy to spend it all in the first shop

column2: a residential trip or school camp away from home
column3: pack with a parent, label your things and talk to a teacher if you feel homesick
column4: feeling homesick is normal and usually passes quickly

column2: the head count on a trip
column3: stand still and answer when the teacher counts
column4: teachers must check that nobody is missing

column2: borrowing a book from the school library
column3: scan or sign it out and return it by the due date
column4: others are waiting for it, and libraries track every book

column2: in the library
column3: talk quietly and walk
column4: other people are reading and working

column2: looking after a library book
column3: keep it dry, clean and away from food, and use a bookmark instead of folding pages
column4: books are shared and need to last for many readers

column2: losing or damaging a library book
column3: tell the librarian honestly
column4: you may have to pay for it, but hiding it is worse

column2: choosing a book that is right for you
column3: read the first page; if there are more than about five words you do not know, it may be too hard for now
column4: a book that is just right is enjoyable and still teaches you

column2: not liking a book after a few chapters
column3: it is fine to stop and choose another
column4: reading should be enjoyable; there are many books to try

column2: finding facts for a project
column3: use the library catalogue, non-fiction books, the index and contents pages
column4: good research uses trusted sources

column2: information found on a website
column3: check who wrote it and compare with another trusted source
column4: anyone can put anything online, and some of it is wrong

column2: fiction and non-fiction
column3: know that fiction is made-up stories and non-fiction gives true information
column4: you choose different books for fun and for facts

column2: the public library
column3: ask a parent to help you get your own library card; borrowing is free
column4: libraries let you read many books without buying them

column2: writing in a library book
column3: never write, draw or highlight in it
column4: the book belongs to everyone

column2: book week or World Book Day
column3: join in by dressing as a book character or sharing a favourite book
column4: it celebrates reading together

column2: learning to ride a bike
column3: wear a helmet, practise in a safe place away from traffic, and keep trying after wobbles
column4: everyone falls sometimes while learning, and a helmet protects the head

column2: learning to swim
column3: go to lessons and swim only where a lifeguard or adult is watching
column4: swimming is a life-saving skill, but water is dangerous until you are strong

column2: learning a musical instrument
column3: practise a little every day, even ten minutes
column4: regular short practice builds skill much faster than one long session a week

column2: practice feels boring
column3: set a small goal for each session and notice your progress
column4: seeing improvement keeps you motivated

column2: something feels too hard
column3: break it into small parts and practise the hardest part slowly
column4: slow, careful practice is how skills are built

column2: comparing yourself with a faster learner
column3: compare yourself with how you were last month instead
column4: everybody learns at a different speed

column2: wanting to quit a club or lesson after one week
column3: give it a fair try for several weeks, then decide with a parent
column4: the start is often the hardest part

column2: learning to tie shoelaces or a tie
column3: practise slowly while an adult shows you step by step
column4: watching and copying is how most practical skills are learned

column2: a coach or teacher corrects you
column3: listen and try the correction; it is not a telling-off
column4: feedback helps you improve faster

column2: learning to type on a keyboard
column3: practise with all fingers on the home row
column4: touch typing is much faster in the long run

column2: learning to cook a simple dish
column3: cook with an adult, wash hands, and be careful with knives and hot pans
column4: cooking is a useful skill, but heat and knives can hurt

column2: forgetting what you learned last week
column3: review it briefly a few days later
column4: reviewing at intervals helps memories last

column2: a myth: «some people are just bad at maths»
column3: know that skill in maths grows with practice like any other skill
column4: believing you can improve helps you keep trying

column2: learning a second language at school
column3: use new words often and do not worry about mistakes
column4: speaking, even with mistakes, is how languages are learned

column2: sleep and learning
column3: go to bed at a regular time; children of 9 to 10 need about 9 to 12 hours of sleep
column4: the brain stores what you learned during sleep

column2: the coins of your country
column3: learn them: in the USA penny 1 cent, nickel 5, dime 10, quarter 25; in the UK 1p to £2; in Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Ireland cents and dollar or euro coins
column4: knowing coins lets you pay and check change

column2: a coin's size and its value
column3: look at the number on the coin, not its size; a US dime is smaller than a nickel but worth more
column4: size does not always show value

column2: the 1 and 2 cent coins in Australia, New Zealand and Canada
column3: know that they are no longer used and cash prices are rounded to the nearest 5 or 10 cents
column4: the coins cost more to make than they were worth

column2: finding money on the ground at school
column3: hand it to a teacher or the office
column4: it belongs to someone who may be looking for it

column2: finding a wallet or purse in the street
column3: give it to a parent, a shop or the police without taking anything
column4: the owner may need their cards and money back

column2: putting coins in your mouth
column3: never put coins in your mouth
column4: they are dirty and can choke you

column2: card payments and phone payments
column3: know that tapping a card or phone spends real money from a bank account
column4: money you cannot see is still real and can run out

column2: getting pocket money or an allowance
column3: keep it in a safe place, such as a money box or purse, and keep track of how much you have
column4: you will know what you can afford

column2: spend, save, share
column3: split your pocket money into three parts: some to spend now, some to save, and some to give
column4: this builds good habits for life

column2: spending all your pocket money on the first day
column3: plan and keep some for later in the week
column4: you may want something later and have nothing left

column2: a friend gets more pocket money than you
column3: know that every family decides differently according to what it can afford
column4: comparing makes you unhappy and money is not a sign of how much you are loved

column2: asking for more pocket money
column3: explain calmly why, and accept the answer
column4: parents decide based on the whole family budget

column2: losing pocket money
column3: keep money zipped in a bag or pocket and do not carry more than you need
column4: lost cash is rarely found again

column2: saving for something you want
column3: write down the price, how much you have, and how many weeks you need
column4: a plan makes the goal feel reachable

column2: a money box or piggy bank
column3: put money in it regularly and do not keep opening it
column4: small amounts add up over time

column2: a children's savings account at a bank
column3: ask a parent to help open one; the bank adds interest
column4: interest is extra money the bank pays you for keeping your money there

column2: wanting to spend your savings on something on impulse
column3: wait a day or a week before buying
column4: if you still want it later, it is a better choice; many wants pass

column2: a goal that takes a long time
column3: celebrate halfway and keep going
column4: reaching a goal you worked for feels good

column2: choosing between two things you want
column3: think which you will use or enjoy longer
column4: money spent on one thing cannot be spent on another

column2: wants and needs
column3: know that needs are things you must have, like food, water, shelter and clothes, and wants are nice extras, like toys and sweets
column4: needs come first when money is limited

column2: seeing an advert for a toy
column3: remember that adverts are made to make you want things and may make them look better than they are
column4: advertisers are paid to sell, not to tell the whole truth

column2: wanting something because everyone else has it
column3: ask yourself if you really want it or only want to fit in
column4: things bought only to fit in often bring little joy

column2: comparing prices in shops
column3: check the price in two places and compare the price per item or per weight
column4: the bigger packet is not always cheaper

column2: a «buy one get one free» offer
column3: buy it only if you would use both
column4: a bargain is not a bargain if you did not need it

column2: cheap toys that break quickly
column3: consider paying a little more for something that lasts
column4: cheap items that break cost more in the end

column2: in-app purchases in games
column3: never buy anything in a game or app without asking a parent first
column4: it spends real money, often the family's card

column2: free games that keep asking you to pay
column3: know they are designed to make you spend small amounts often
column4: small payments quickly add up to a lot

column2: loot boxes and mystery packs
column3: know they are like gambling: you pay without knowing what you get
column4: you often spend a lot and get things you do not want

column2: buying something online
column3: ask a parent and only buy from websites they trust
column4: some websites are scams and never send the item

column2: a pop-up says you have won a prize
column3: do not click it and tell a parent
column4: it is almost always a trick to get personal information or money

column2: someone online asks for a gift card or money
column3: never send it; tell a parent straight away
column4: scammers ask for gift cards because they cannot be traced

column2: keeping a receipt
column3: keep the receipt until you are sure the item works
column4: you need it to return or exchange something

column2: a bought toy is broken in the box
column3: take it back with the receipt to exchange it or get a refund
column4: shops must replace or refund faulty items

column2: sales tax in the USA
column3: know that the price on the shelf in most US states does not include tax, which is added at the till
column4: you need a little more money than the label shows

column2: prices in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand
column3: know that the price on the label already includes tax
column4: what you see is what you pay

column2: paying at a shop counter
column3: have your money ready, say hello, please and thank you
column4: it is polite and quicker for everyone in the queue

column2: working out change
column3: count up from the price to the amount you gave
column4: this is how you check you got the right change

column2: getting too much change
column3: tell the shop assistant and give back the extra
column4: it is honest, and the assistant may have to pay the difference

column2: getting too little change
column3: politely say you think the change is wrong and count it together
column4: mistakes happen and are easily fixed at the counter

column2: not having enough money at the till
column3: politely put something back
column4: it is normal and nothing to be embarrassed about

column2: estimating the total before paying
column3: round each price and add them in your head
column4: you will know if you have enough before you reach the till

column2: a price like $4.99
column3: know that it is almost $5, not $4
column4: shops use such prices to make things seem cheaper

column2: buying from an ice-cream van or school tuck shop
column3: check the price list first and hold your money ready
column4: you will not be surprised by the price

column2: a friend asks to borrow money
column3: lend only a small amount you can afford to lose and agree when it will be paid back
column4: friends sometimes forget, and money can spoil friendships

column2: you borrow money from a friend
column3: pay it back on time without being reminded
column4: paying back keeps trust

column2: a friend has not paid back money
column3: remind them kindly, and ask a parent for advice if it continues
column4: a gentle reminder usually works

column2: borrowing money from a parent for something now
column3: agree how and when you will pay it back from pocket money
column4: this is like a small loan and teaches what debt means

column2: an older child demands your money
column3: give it if you feel unsafe, then tell a trusted adult straight away
column4: this is bullying or theft and adults must stop it

column2: what a loan is
column3: know that a loan is money you borrow and must pay back, often with extra called interest
column4: borrowing costs money, so adults borrow carefully

column2: taking money from a parent's purse without asking
column3: never take money without permission
column4: it is stealing, even at home

column2: lending a book or game to a friend
column3: lend it if you trust them, and say when you need it back
column4: clear agreements prevent arguments

column2: reading an analogue clock
column3: the short hand shows the hour and the long hand the minutes; each number on the face means 5 minutes
column4: many clocks at school and in public places have hands

column2: half past, quarter past and quarter to
column3: half past 3 is 3:30, quarter past 3 is 3:15, quarter to 4 is 3:45
column4: people say times this way in everyday speech

column2: a.m. and p.m.
column3: a.m. is from midnight to midday, p.m. from midday to midnight
column4: 7 a.m. is morning and 7 p.m. is evening, a big difference

column2: the 24-hour clock
column3: 15:00 is 3 p.m.; subtract 12 from hours after 12
column4: timetables for trains, buses and planes in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand often use it

column2: the clocks change for daylight saving time
column3: change clocks forward one hour in spring and back one hour in autumn: «spring forward, fall back»
column4: forgetting makes you an hour early or late; the dates differ between the northern and southern hemispheres

column2: time zones
column3: know that the USA, Canada and Australia have several time zones, so it can be a different time in another part of the country
column4: phoning relatives far away needs a check of their time

column2: working out how long something takes
column3: count on from the start time to the end time in hours and minutes
column4: this tells you when you must start to finish on time

column2: the days of the week and months of the year
column3: learn them in order, and use the rhyme «thirty days has September, April, June and November» for month lengths
column4: you need them to plan and find dates

column2: a leap year
column3: know that February has 29 days every four years
column4: the Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go round the Sun

column2: seasons in the south
column3: know that in Australia and New Zealand summer is December to February and Christmas is in summer
column4: the seasons are opposite in the southern hemisphere

column2: writing the date
column3: in the UK, Ireland, Australia and New Zealand 3/4 is 3 April; in the USA it is March 4
column4: the order of day and month differs and can cause mix-ups

column2: a family calendar on the fridge
column3: write your events on it, such as games, parties and trips
column4: everyone can see what is planned and avoid clashes

column2: school terms and holidays
column3: know when your terms start and end: four terms in Australia and New Zealand, three in the UK and Ireland, two semesters in many US schools
column4: you can plan and look forward to breaks

column2: being late for a friend's party or game
column3: leave earlier than you think you need
column4: being late makes others wait and you miss the start

column2: knowing you will be late
column3: tell the person as soon as you can
column4: it is polite and they do not worry

column2: losing track of time while playing
column3: set a timer or alarm for when you must go home
column4: parents worry when you do not come home when agreed

column2: being told «be home by dusk»
column3: check when the sun sets that day, as it changes with the seasons
column4: in winter it gets dark much earlier

column2: waiting for someone who is late
column3: wait a reasonable time and then ask an adult what to do
column4: everyone is sometimes late, but you must not be left alone for long

column2: a free Saturday
column3: make a simple plan: jobs first, then fun
column4: getting jobs done first lets you enjoy free time without worry

column2: too many things to do
column3: write a list and do the most important things first
column4: a list stops you forgetting and shows what matters most

column2: guessing how long jobs take
column3: time yourself once to see how long things really take
column4: most people think jobs are quicker than they are

column2: the weather changes your plans
column3: have a backup plan for rainy days
column4: being flexible avoids disappointment

column2: boredom on a free day
column3: read, draw, build, play outside or help at home
column4: boredom often leads to creativity

column2: a morning routine
column3: do the same steps in the same order: get up, wash, dress, breakfast, teeth, bag
column4: a routine makes mornings quicker and calmer

column2: an evening routine
column3: bath or shower, pyjamas, teeth, reading, then lights off at the same time each night
column4: a regular bedtime helps you fall asleep and feel fresh at school

column2: brushing teeth
column3: brush for two minutes twice a day, in the morning and before bed
column4: it prevents tooth decay

column2: weekends and holidays
column3: keep bedtime close to the normal one
column4: very late nights make returning to school hard

column2: how much screen time is fine
column3: follow your family's screen rules and balance screens with outdoor play, reading and sleep
column4: too much screen time takes time away from sleep, movement and friends

column2: screens before bed
column3: switch off screens at least an hour before sleep and keep devices out of the bedroom at night
column4: bright screens and exciting games make it harder to fall asleep

column2: «just one more episode or level»
column3: stop when the agreed time is up, using a timer
column4: games and videos are designed to keep you watching

column2: autoplay on video apps
column3: turn it off or stop after your chosen video
column4: autoplay keeps you watching longer than you planned

column2: feeling cross when the screen is turned off
column3: take a few breaths and move on to another activity
column4: the feeling passes quickly

column2: social media age limits
column3: know that most social media apps require you to be at least 13
column4: they are not designed for younger children and can expose them to harm

column2: playing online games with strangers
column3: never share your real name, school, address or photos and tell a parent if anyone makes you uncomfortable
column4: people online may not be who they say they are

column2: eyes tired after a long time on a screen
column3: take regular breaks and look into the distance
column4: breaks help the eyes and body rest

column2: being asked to help at home
column3: help willingly, for example setting the table, making your bed or feeding a pet
column4: everyone in a family shares the work of a home

column2: doing a chore badly so you will not be asked again
column3: do it properly
column4: doing a job well builds trust and you learn useful skills

column2: earning extra pocket money
column3: offer to do extra jobs, such as washing the car or weeding, and agree the payment first
column4: agreeing first prevents arguments

column2: selling things at a lemonade stand or bake sale
column3: do it with an adult's help, wash hands and price things clearly
column4: it teaches earning, counting money and talking to customers

column2: selling old toys
column3: ask a parent first and agree a fair price
column4: parents may have bought them and should agree

column2: being paid for every little job
column3: know that some jobs are simply part of family life and are not paid
column4: helping your family is not always about money

column2: doing a job for a neighbour
column3: ask a parent first and make sure they know where you are
column4: your safety comes first

column2: what a job and a salary are
column3: know that adults earn money by working, and the money pays for the home, food and bills
column4: money comes from work, not from the card machine

column2: being invited to a birthday party
column3: reply to the invitation by the date asked
column4: the host needs to know how many children are coming

column2: bringing a present to a party
column3: choose something simple and thoughtful; the price is not what matters
column4: it is the thought that counts

column2: getting a present you do not like
column3: say thank you and smile
column4: the giver chose it to please you

column2: thank-you notes after a birthday
column3: write a short thank-you card or message to each giver
column4: it shows gratitude

column2: talking about a party at school
column3: do not talk about it in front of children who were not invited
column4: they may feel left out

column2: a birthday in the class
column3: sing «Happy Birthday» and wish them a good day
column4: it makes the birthday child feel special

column2: blowing out the candles
column3: make a wish and blow them out, without spitting
column4: it is a fun tradition, and others will eat the cake

column2: Thanksgiving in the USA and Canada
column3: know that families gather for a big meal and give thanks; it is in November in the USA and October in Canada
column4: it is one of the biggest family holidays in North America

column2: Halloween trick-or-treating on 31 October
column3: go with an adult, visit only houses with lights on and check treats before eating
column4: safety comes first in the dark and among traffic

column2: Bonfire Night on 5 November in the UK
column3: watch fireworks only at organised displays and stand well back
column4: fireworks can cause bad burns

column2: Fourth of July fireworks in the USA
column3: never touch fireworks or sparklers without adult supervision
column4: sparklers burn much hotter than a candle

column2: St Patrick's Day on 17 March
column3: know that it is Ireland's national day, celebrated with parades and green clothes
column4: it honours the patron saint of Ireland

column2: Anzac Day on 25 April in Australia and New Zealand
column3: stand quietly during the minute's silence and dawn services
column4: it remembers the soldiers who died in wars

column2: Remembrance Day on 11 November
column3: stand still and silent during the two-minute silence and wear a poppy if you wish
column4: it honours those who died in wars

column2: Waitangi Day on 6 February in New Zealand
column3: know that it marks the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi between Māori and the British Crown
column4: it is New Zealand's national day

column2: religious and cultural festivals in class
column3: be respectful when classmates celebrate Christmas, Diwali, Eid, Hanukkah or Lunar New Year
column4: everyone's traditions deserve respect

column2: getting Christmas presents
column3: be grateful, and remember that not every family can afford many presents
column4: kindness and gratitude matter more than the number of gifts

column2: the long summer holiday
column3: keep reading and doing a little practice
column4: this stops you forgetting what you learned
